title: Reading GPU entries from the device specifications table using a nested dict lookup
reading_goal: Accurately interpret the parallel computing characteristics associated with the GPU using nested dictionary lookups.
code:
devices = {
    "CPU": {"strength": "general control flow"},
    "GPU": {"strength": "massively parallel numeric work"},
    "TPU": {"strength": "tensor workloads"},
    "NPU": {"strength": "efficient AI inference"},
}
gpu_strength = devices["GPU"]["strength"]
print(gpu_strength)
question: What are the GPU characteristics that the `target` expression reads?
choices: Strong at processing many numeric operations in parallel.
Exclusive control over all branch handling in the operating system
Specialized exclusively for saving text files
It always consumes more power than the CPU.
answer: Strong at processing many numeric operations in parallel.
explanation: 1) Check the strength of multiple devices in the `devices` dictionary. 2) `devices['GPU']` selects the dictionary containing GPU information. 3) Retrieve the descriptive string for the `strength` entry in that dictionary. 4) The string is stored in `gpu_strength`.
project_context: Understanding the nature of the workload is fundamental to determining whether to deploy model training and inference tasks on a CPU or a GPU.
reading_goal_internal: nested dict lookup으로 GPU에 연결된 병렬 계산 특성을 정확히 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A nested dict subscription first retrieves a value from the outer dict and then looks up the key again in the resulting dict.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Read `devices['GPU']` as returning the GPU-info dict, then the following `['strength']` as extracting the description string.
concept_explanation.key_point: The practical advantage of GPUs lies in their ability to apply the same type of numerical and matrix operations in parallel to a very large number of tasks.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: You should not generalize that GPUs are automatically faster than CPUs in all programs. Their advantages vary depending on the nature of the task.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The first subscription selects the "GPU" sub-dict, and the second selects the "role" value.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Check the strength of multiple devices in the `devices` dictionary. 2) `devices['GPU']` selects the dictionary containing GPU information. 3) Retrieve the descriptive string for the `strength` entry in that dictionary. 4) The string is stored in `gpu_strength`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The practical advantage of GPUs lies in their ability to apply the same type of numerical and matrix operations in parallel to a very large number of tasks.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Exclusive control over all branch handling in the operating system
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: In cases involving complex control flow and general-purpose execution, the CPU typically plays a more central role.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Don’t judge the relative merits based solely on device names; instead, analyze the workload characteristics.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Compute comparison data is read in the order **device key → attribute key → actual workload description**.

title: Reading the General-Purpose Control Flow of a CPU That Selects Different Tasks via Branches
reading_goal: Read that the structure—which directs different operations along conditional paths based on the execution order of if/elif/else branches—demonstrates the CPU’s role in general-purpose control.
question: Why does this code, which uses `if/elif/else` to split handling paths for `download`, `parse`, and other work, demonstrate the general-purpose role of a CPU?
choices: Because it evaluates different task types based on conditions and sends them into different control flows.
Because the same numerical operations are applied simultaneously to thousands of data points,
Since we are directly measuring GPU memory usage,
Since all branches are executed simultaneously and the results are combined,
answer: Because it evaluates different task types based on conditions and sends them into different control flows.
explanation: 1) “parse” is entered. 2) The “download” condition fails. 3) The “parse” condition evaluates to true, and the parser path is selected. 4) This kind of general-purpose control flow—which routes different types of tasks to different paths based on conditions—is an example of the CPU’s role.
project_context: This is used when linking general program control flow—which selects different handlers based on file format, task type, and user requests—to the role of the CPU.
reading_goal_internal: `if/elif/else`가 서로 다른 작업 종류에 따라 실행 경로를 선택하는 구조를 읽고, 이를 CPU가 강한 범용 분기·제어 흐름의 예로 연결한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The `elif` clause selects the execution path by checking the next condition when the preceding `if` condition is False.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: `task_type` Read the control flow, which checks whether a value matches certain conditions in sequence and selects a single processing path accordingly.
concept_explanation.key_point: The key point of this example is not that multiple types of tasks are processed in parallel using the same operation, but rather that different processing paths are selected based on conditions; this general-purpose branching and control flow aligns well with the role of the CPU.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: If you simply identify which branch `handle("parse")` takes and stop there, you’ll miss why this branching code was used to compare CPU roles.

teaching_example.walkthrough: If the image comparison is False and the text comparison is True, `tokenize` is returned, and the `else` block is not executed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) When `handle("parse")` is called, `task_type` is "parse." 2) The "download" condition in the first `if` statement is False. 3) `elif task_type == "parse"` evaluates to True, so the parser path is selected. 4) In other words, this function determines the input type to select different task paths, and this general-purpose branching and control flow is an example of the CPU’s role.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The objective is to understand, in conjunction with the code flow, that the CPU excels at its general-purpose role of handling various types of tasks, as well as branches and control flow.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Because the same numerical operations are applied simultaneously to thousands of data points,
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: That description is closer to the characteristics of GPUs, which excel at large-scale parallel numerical computations, and the current code selects different paths depending on the conditions.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Don’t just look at the selected branch; verify that the nature of the workload performed by the code involves “assessing and controlling various conditions.”

answer_explanation.takeaway: The example of the CPU’s role should be interpreted as a general-purpose control flow, such as **multiple types of tasks → conditional evaluation → selection of different execution paths**.

title: Reading Matrix Multiplication Using the @ Operator
reading_goal: `a @ b` Interpret this as a matrix multiplication expression and separate the context of GPU tensor calculations from Python’s arithmetic syntax.
code:
import torch

a = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="cuda")
b = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="cuda")
c = a @ b
question: `a @ b` Which of the following is the correct operation represented by ?
explanation: The `torch.randn` call creates the tensors `a` and `b`. Both tensors are placed on the CUDA device. ``a @ b`` computes the matrix product of the two tensors, and the result is stored in `c`. This is because in Python, the ``@`` operator represents matrix multiplication. Common source of confusion: String concatenation. String concatenation typically uses ``+``, but in this case, `a` and `b` are tensors. Point of confusion: You must consider both the operator symbol ``@`` and the types of the operands. ``left @ right`` is a matrix multiplication expression between objects that support ``@``.
project_context: This card explains how to distinguish between Python’s ``@`` syntax and the context of device acceleration when reading large matrix operations involving GPU tensors in deep learning code.
reading_goal_internal: `a @ b`를 matrix multiplication 표현식으로 읽고 GPU tensor 계산 맥락과 Python 연산 문법을 분리한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `@` is Python’s matrix multiplication operator. When used between objects that support this operation, it evaluates as matrix or tensor multiplication.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, determine what kind of objects `a` on the left and `b` on the right are, and then read that ``a @ b`` performs the matrix multiplication of those two.
concept_explanation.key_point: Whether or not a GPU is used depends on the context of the library and device; the focus of the Python syntax is on matrix multiplication, as indicated by ``@``.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `@` It is easy to mistake this for a standard multiplication operation like ``*``. The two operators use different methods and have different meanings.

teaching_example.walkthrough: If `features` and `weights` are matrix objects that support ``@``, the matrix product is calculated on the right side, and the result is stored in `scores`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The `torch.randn` call creates the tensors `a` and `b`. Both tensors are placed on a CUDA device. `a @ b` produces the result of the matrix multiplication of the two tensors, and that result is stored in `c`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: In Python, the ``@`` operator represents matrix multiplication.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: String concatenation typically uses `+`, and in this case, a and b are tensors.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: You must consider both the operator symbol `@` and the type of the operand object.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `left @ right``@` is a matrix multiplication expression between objects that support .

title: Retrieving Values from the Accelerator Information Dict
reading_goal: Track the flow of reading a specific key value from the accelerator metadata using a `dict` subscription and storing the result in a variable.
question: What value does the last line output?
explanation: In the `accelerator` dictionary, the value for `name` is `TPU`, and the value for `best_for` is `tensor_matrix_ops`. Since the square bracket lookup selects the `best_for` key, `workload` is set to `tensor_matrix_ops`. The `print` statement outputs that value because ``accelerator["best_for"]`` in the dictionary returns the value associated with the `best_for` key. Common misconception: `best_for` is the name of the key used for the lookup, and what is printed is the value associated with that key. Point of confusion: You must distinguish between the key inside the square brackets and the value returned by the lookup. ``mapping[key]`` reads the value associated with that key, not the key name itself.
project_context: This refers to the context of reading the necessary items from Python data that organizes the characteristics of various accelerators—such as GPUs, TPUs, and NPUs—as metadata.
reading_goal_internal: dict subscription으로 가속기 metadata의 특정 key 값을 읽고 결과가 변수에 저장되는 흐름을 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A `dict` subscription is a syntax that reads the value associated with a specific key in the form `dictionary[key]`.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check which keys are present in the `accelerator`, and then read that ``accelerator["best_for"]`` retrieves the value of `best_for`.
concept_explanation.key_point: TPU is a coverage context, and the Python focus is on the subscription that retrieves a value from a dict using a key.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to mistakenly think that the string inside the square brackets is the result itself. "best_for" is the key to be found, and the result is the value associated with that key.

teaching_example.walkthrough: "use" is the key, and the value "inference" associated with that key is stored in the job.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: In the `accelerator` dictionary, the value for `name` is `TPU`, and the value for `best_for` is `tensor_matrix_ops`. Since the bracket lookup selects the `best_for` key, `tensor_matrix_ops` is stored under `workload`. The `print` statement outputs that value.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because `accelerator["best_for"]` in `dict` returns the value of the `best_for` key.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `best_for` is the name of the key used for the lookup, and the value associated with that key is what is output.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: You must distinguish between the `key` inside the brackets and the `value` returned by the query.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `mapping[key]` reads the value associated with the key, not the key name itself.

title: Checking two device conditions together using “and”
reading_goal: The results of the two dict lookups are combined using ``and`` to check whether all device conditions are met.
question: What value does the last line output?
explanation: The value of the `on_device` key in `device` is `True`. Since the left side is true, the `and` operator also evaluates the `low_power` value, which is also `True`. Because both conditions are true, `suitable` becomes `True`. This is because both operands connected by ``and`` are true. Common mistake: False. Neither of the two keys has a value of False. Point of confusion: You must check the actual dictionary values on both sides of the `and` operator. ``A and B`` is a boolean operation that evaluates to True only when both A and B are True.
project_context: This context involves checking various characteristics of an edge AI device using Python metadata to determine execution conditions.
reading_goal_internal: 두 dict lookup 결과를 `and`로 결합해 장치 조건이 모두 충족되는지 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `and` is a boolean operation that evaluates both the left and right conditions. The overall condition is true only when both are true.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, it checks the value on the left (`device["on_device"]`), and if it is true, it also checks the value on the right (`device["low_power"]`).
concept_explanation.key_point: NPU refers to a product and hardware context, while the Python focus is a logical operation that combines two conditions using `and`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think the whole expression is True when only one of the two conditions is True. That rule is closer to `or`; with `and`, both conditions must be true.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `enabled` is True but `verified` is False, the overall result of the `and` condition is False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The value of the `on_device` key for `device` is `True`. Since the left side is true, the `and` operator also checks the `low_power` value, which is also `True`. Since both conditions are true, `suitable` becomes `True`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because both operands connected by `and` are True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: None of the two keys have a value of False.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: and you must check the actual dict values on both sides separately.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `A and B` is a Boolean operation that evaluates to true when both A and B are true.

title: Using dictionary comprehensions to transfer each input tensor to CUDA
reading_goal: Read the iterable, keys, and value expressions in a dictionary comprehension in order.
code:
# CPU side
text = load_text("prompt.txt")
inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")

# GPU side
inputs = {k: v.to("cuda") for k, v in inputs.items()}
outputs = model.generate(**inputs)
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate result produced by this dict comprehension?
choices: A new dictionary containing the original key and the value converted to CUDA
answer: A new dictionary containing the original key and the value converted to CUDA
explanation: The comprehension iterates over `inputs.items()`. Each key remains `k`, while each value is replaced by the result of `v.to("cuda")`. Those key-value pairs are collected into a new dictionary. Because the outer form of the dict comprehension is `{k: expression for ...}`, the resulting data structure is a dict. Common wrong answer: the single string `"cuda"`. That string is only an argument passed to each `.to()` call; it is not the result of the whole comprehension.
project_context: This connects to reading code that moves multiple tensors in a tokenizer result dict to the same GPU device before model inference.
reading_goal_internal: dict comprehension의 반복 대상, key, value 변환식을 순서대로 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A dict comprehension takes items one by one from an iterable and creates a new dict from `key: value` pairs.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It is read as: “Iterate through the items using `for k, v in inputs.items()`; keep each key as is, and assign the result of `v.to("cuda")` to the value.”
concept_explanation.key_point: This is not a statement that modifies the existing dict item by item; it is **an expression that creates a new dict**.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `v.to("cuda")` It’s easy to assume that a single call returns a single tensor. However, a comprehension collects the results of all items to create a dictionary.

teaching_example.code:
words = {"a": "ONE", "b": "TWO"}
lower = {k: v.lower() for k, v in words.items()}
teaching_example.walkthrough: Create a new dict that keeps each key and applies `lower()` to each corresponding value.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `comprehension` iterates through ``inputs.items()``. Each key is retained as ``k``, and the value is replaced with the result of calling ``v.to("cuda")``. These key-value pairs are collected to create a new dictionary.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the outer form of a dict comprehension is `{k: transformed_value for ...}`, the resulting data structure is a dict.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `"cuda"` is merely an argument passed to each `.to()` call; it is not the result of the entire comprehension.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the arguments of an inner call were confused with the result data structure of the outer comprehension.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A dictionary comprehension is read in the following order: **iteration → key/value calculation → construction of a new dictionary**.

target_statement: inputs = {k: v.to("cuda") for k, v in inputs.items()}
focus_span: {k: v.to("cuda") for k, v in inputs.items()}

title: batch.to("cuda") Store the return value back into batch
reading_goal: Track, in order, the return value of a method call and the value used in the next model call after reassignment.
question: `model(batch)` What is the value of the ``batch`` used here?
choices: Always use the original batch before starting each iteration
explanation: The call to ``batch.to("cuda")`` on the right is evaluated first. Since its result is stored back into ``batch`` on the left, reading the same name on the next line uses the new return value. This is because Python assignment evaluates the right-hand side first and stores the result in the left-hand name. A common source of confusion: The name ``batch`` is always reassigned with the method’s return value in the middle line of the original batch before the loop begins. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when you overlook the step where the reference target of the same variable name changes after the reassignment. ``x = x.method()`` is read in the following order: **call with the existing `x` → receive the return value → store it back in `x`**.
project_context: This connects to understanding what the actual model input variables point to after a device move in a GPU inference loop.
reading_goal_internal: 메서드 호출의 반환값과 재대입 이후 다음 모델 호출에 쓰이는 값을 순서대로 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `object.method(...)` calls a method on an object and can receive its return value as the result.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It reads as: "First, call `batch.to("cuda")`, and then store the return value back into the `batch` on the left."
concept_explanation.key_point: The `batch` in the next line refers to **the reassigned return value, not the variable’s value before the method call**.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `.to()` It’s easy to overlook the left-hand reassignment when looking only at the call. In this code, the result of the call is reassigned to a variable with the same name, ``batch``.

teaching_example.walkthrough: After receiving the result of the method call on the right, store it back into the same variable, ``item``.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The call to ``batch.to("cuda")`` on the right is evaluated first. Since its result is stored back into ``batch`` on the left, reading the same name on the next line uses the new return value.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because Python evaluation evaluates the right-hand side first and stores the result in the left-hand side variable.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Always use the original batch before starting each iteration
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: In the middle line, the name ``batch`` is reassigned as the method’s return value.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of a case where the learner missed the step where the reference target of a variable with the same name changed after reassignment.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `x = x.method()` It is read in the following order: **call the existing x → receive the return value → store it back in x**.

title: Reading Matrix Multiplication Using the @ Operator
reading_goal: Read the right-hand side of the input statement to understand that ``@`` refers to matrix multiplication—not the standard multiplication ``*``.
code:
# many independent scores
scores = embeddings @ query_vector
question: In `scores = embeddings @ query_vector`, what operation does the `@` symbol represent?
explanation: First, look at the right-hand side: ``embeddings @ query_vector``. The middle expression, ``@``, is Python’s matrix multiplication operator, and the result of the calculation is stored in the left-hand side: ``scores``. This is because, in Python syntax, ``@`` is the operator defined for matrix multiplication. A common source of confusion: The remainder operation is calculated using the ``%`` operator. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the operator symbol itself is not distinguished. When looking at ``a @ b``, it is read as **matrix multiplication**.
project_context: This relates to quickly identifying the `@` operator in code that calculates similarity scores for embedding vectors all at once.
reading_goal_internal: 대입문의 오른쪽에서 `@`가 일반 곱셈 `*`이 아니라 행렬 곱을 뜻한다는 점을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The Python ``@`` operator is used to represent matrix multiplication.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: `embeddings @ query_vector` is read as a matrix multiplication of `embeddings` and `query_vector`.
concept_explanation.key_point: `@` is an operator distinct from `*`, which denotes element-wise multiplication.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to mistake `@` for a mere ornament or the standard multiplication symbol. In Python, it is a separate matrix multiplication operator.

teaching_example.code:
import numpy as np

matrix = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
vector = np.array([5, 6])
result = matrix @ vector
teaching_example.walkthrough: In the ``matrix @ vector`` on the right, perform a matrix multiplication on ``@`` and store the result in ``result``.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: First, look at `embeddings @ query_vector` on the right. The `@` in the middle is Python’s matrix multiplication operator, and the calculated result is stored in `scores` on the left.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because, in Python syntax, ``@`` is an operator defined for matrix multiplication.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The rest is calculated using the `%` operator.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the operator symbols themselves were not distinguished.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `a @ b` When you see this, read it as **matrix multiplication**.

title: Checking the `elif` condition when the preceding `if` is false
reading_goal: Track the order in which the elif conditions are evaluated in an if/elif/else structure, following the execution sequence.
question: First, `if`. If the condition is false and `elif status == "retry"` is true, what is stored in `action`?
explanation: Since `status` is `retry`, the `if` condition in the first `ok` statement evaluates to false. The `elif` condition in the next `retry` statement then evaluates to true, causing the assignment statement in that block to execute. This is because the `elif` block that evaluates to true contains `action = "enqueue"`. Commonly Misunderstood Answer: The `else` block is executed only when both the preceding `if` and `elif` blocks evaluate to false. Common misinterpretation: This occurs when a reader mistakenly believes that execution continues to the `elif` block even after an `else` evaluates to true. An `elif` **checks the preceding condition only when it is false**; if it is true, it executes that block and skips the subsequent branch.
project_context: This ties into reading CPU scheduling code that selects different processing methods based on state, such as batching, queues, and retries.
reading_goal_internal: if/elif/else 구조에서 elif 조건이 검사되는 시점을 실행 순서대로 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `elif` This is a branch that checks the following condition when the preceding ``if`` or ``elif`` condition is false.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Read the conditions from the top down; the code proceeds to the current condition—`elif`—only if the preceding condition is false.
concept_explanation.key_point: If the preceding `if` condition is already true, this `elif` condition is not evaluated.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think every condition is always checked separately. Once one branch is selected, the later branches are skipped.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the first ``if`` is false, it checks ``elif state == "waiting"``. Since this condition is true, it stores ``pending`` in ``label``.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Since `status` is `retry`, the `if` condition in the first `ok` statement evaluates to false. The `elif` condition in the next `retry` statement then evaluates to true, causing the assignment statement in that block to execute.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because ``action = "enqueue"`` is contained within the ``elif`` block, which has become `True`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `else` is executed only when both the preceding ``if`` and ``elif`` are false.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: `elif` This is an example of a misreading where the code continues down to ``else`` even after the condition becomes true.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `elif` **Checks only when the preceding condition is false**; if it is true, it executes that block and then skips the subsequent branch.

title: Calculating the product of batch size and input length

title: Combine the two performance signals using “and” to identify potential bottlenecks
reading_goal: Evaluate the conditions of low GPU utilization and a backlogged CPU queue separately, and then interpret the results.
code:
gpu_util = 15
cpu_queue = 6
cpu_or_io_bottleneck = gpu_util < 30 and cpu_queue > 0
question: What is the value of `cpu_or_io_bottleneck`?
explanation: The first comparison is True, and the second comparison is also True. Since both conditions are true, `and` evaluates to True. This is because both conditions of the Boolean `and` operator are True. Commonly confused incorrect answer: False. Currently, neither of the two comparisons is false. Common misinterpretation: This occurs when one of the comparisons is calculated incorrectly or the `and` rule is applied incorrectly. The performance diagnostic condition should be read as **comparison of each signal → Boolean combination**.
project_context: This connects to the workflow of checking other potential bottlenecks—such as CPU preprocessing, disk I/O, and small batch sizes—in batch jobs with low GPU utilization.

title: Selecting an accelerator suited to your workload: Reading the mapping

question: What is the best choice for deep learning training that involves many large matrix multiplications?
choices: Only a single core of the CPU
explanation: In the “mapping” section, large matrix multiplication is associated with GPU_or_TPU. This is because these devices provide execution resources specialized for large-scale parallel numerical computations. A common source of confusion: Selecting “only a single CPU core” is an incorrect answer because it fails to take advantage of the parallelism inherent in large matrix multiplication. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the parallel processing characteristics of the workload are not considered. title: Read: Why GPUs Do Not Automatically Accelerate File I/O-Intensive Python Loops
reading_goal: Determine whether the loop body consists of GPU-friendly matrix operations or is CPU/file I/O-intensive to identify the bottleneck.
code:
rows = []
for file in files:
    text = file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    rows.append(parse(text))
question: Why is it difficult to significantly speed up this code using only the GPU?
choices: Because there are too many matrix multiplications
Because the NPU processes it automatically
This is because the focus is on file I/O and Python control flow.
answer: This is because the focus is on file I/O and Python control flow.
explanation: The core of the loop is the process of reading a file and parsing it using Python functions. There are no large-scale tensor operations for the GPU. This is because accelerators only provide a benefit when the workload is actually executed on that device. A common source of confusion: “Because there are too many matrix multiplies.” There are no matrix multiplies in the code at all. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when a matrix workload is assumed simply because of the AI/performance context. Performance analysis prioritizes identifying **the actual bottleneck location** over the device name.
project_context: This connects to distinguishing I/O, CPU, and Python-overhead bottlenecks rather than looking only at the GPU-utilization number when a batch job is slow.
reading_goal_internal: loop 본문이 GPU-friendly matrix operation인지 CPU/file I/O 중심인지 구분해 bottleneck을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `for file in files:` This is a basic `for` statement that iterates through an iterable one element at a time.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check where the actual time is spent in the body of the code rather than in the loop itself.
concept_explanation.key_point: If disk reads and Python parsing are the primary bottlenecks, adding a GPU will not automatically shift those bottlenecks to GPU kernels.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that having a GPU will automatically speed up all Python code.

teaching_example.code:
rows=[]
for path in paths:
    text=path.read_text()
    rows.append(parse(text))
teaching_example.walkthrough: The main operations are file reading and Python parsing, not matrix kernels.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The core of the loop is reading a file and parsing it using a Python function. There are no large-scale tensor operations for the GPU.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Accelerators provide a performance benefit because the workload actually runs on that device.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Because there are too many matrix multiplications
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: There is absolutely no matrix multiplication in the code.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where a matrix workload is assumed solely because of the AI/performance context.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Performance analysis first identifies **the actual location of the bottleneck** rather than the device name.
